record.paper_title: Chapter 15: Open Questions and Future Directions in Titan Science
record.original_question: What is Titan's internal differentiated structure, including the composition and layering of its hydrosphere, refractory core, ocean, ice shell, and any high-pressure water-ice layer, and can future gravity, surface-deformation, and seismic measurements resolve the discrepancies in inferred ocean density and interior layering?

evidence.quote: 4) What is the internal state of differentiation including the core?

Strong evidence for differentiation within Titan comes from gravity measurements, which provide values for the Moment of Inertia (MoI) and the degree 2 tidal Love number. The MoI suggests that Titan is differentiated into a hydrosphere and a refractory core.

A major question, which also affects the habitability of the ocean, concerns the presence and properties of a high pressure water ice layer (or layers) at the base of the ocean (Journaux et al., 2017, 2020; Kalousová and Sotin, 2020a), affecting the exchange of core materials with the ocean (Miller et al., 2019).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Saturn's largest moon, Titan, is believed to be a differentiated body comprising (from the center outward) a refractory rocky/metallic core, possibly a high-pressure water-ice layer, a subsurface liquid water (or water-ammonia) ocean, and an outer ice-I shell. Available constraints on its interior come primarily from the polar moment of inertia C/(MR^2) and the degree-2 tidal Love numbers k_2 and h_2 inferred from gravity tracking, together with rotational state and topography.

Determine Titan's internal differentiated structure: namely, specify the radii, thicknesses, densities, and compositions of
  (i) the refractory core,
  (ii) any high-pressure water-ice layer at the base of the ocean (its presence, number of phases, thickness, and whether it permits chemical exchange between the core and the ocean),
  (iii) the subsurface ocean (thickness, density, salinity/ammonia content),
  (iv) the outer ice-I shell (thickness and rheology),
in a manner consistent with the measured mean density, moment-of-inertia factor, and tidal Love numbers, and reconcile the existing discrepancies in inferred ocean density and layering.

Additionally, assess whether future measurements—improved static and time-variable gravity field coefficients, surface-deformation amplitudes (tidal h_2 and rotational variations), and seismic observations of body-wave travel times and normal-mode frequencies—are sufficient, in principle, to uniquely resolve the above interior parameters.
artifact.status_search_result: Titan's detailed interior differentiation remains unresolved. Cassini-era gravity and rotation data constrain bulk parameters but admit multiple interior models (with or without a high-pressure ice layer, varying ocean densities, and partially differentiated cores). The upcoming Dragonfly mission and proposed orbiters/seismic packages are anticipated to improve constraints, but as of 2026 no consensus model exists.

status_evidence.title: Titan's interior structure - review
status_evidence.snippet: Open questions remain regarding Titan's core differentiation, the presence of a high-pressure ice layer, and ocean composition.
status_evidence.claim: The interior differentiation of Titan is listed among the open questions for future Titan science.
